transcript: [00:00] Lena Park (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Raj Patel (Acme): Raj here, Maya, Tom — hi all.
[00:15] Miguel Santos (Redwood): Miguel from Redwood infra/SE team. We'll focus on embedding dims, batch sizing, KV caching, quantization tradeoffs and cost.
[01:02] Maya Chen (Acme): Super, our immediate goal is reranking for patient record search, tight latency — 50 to 150 ms per query tail ideally, and cost matters, we have ~100 QPS peak for rerank.
[02:10] Tom Rivers (Acme): Also important: we need VPC/on-prem options for PHI and KMS integration for keys. We'll want audit logs etc.
[03:00] Lena Park (Redwood): Totally — we'll cover Private/Dedicated constraints. First, can you share vector dims you're currently using? Maya:

[03:15] Maya Chen (Acme): Right now we build 512 dim embeddings using an open model, store them in our vector DB. But we see cost and latency for batch rerank is high, and recall is fine but ranking precision not great on shorter queries.

[04:02] Miguel Santos (Redwood): Two quick axes: dimension and model type (dense vs quantized). Lower dims like 256 or 128 can drop cost and memory and improve CPU/GPU throughput but you trade some accuracy. We can run an eval with your labeled set to quantify delta.

[05:20] Raj Patel (Acme): What's the impact on latency SLOs for different batch sizes? Our pipeline does a candidate generation (vector DB) then a rerank on top-k=100 with cross-encoder-like model, or a dot-product rerank depending on config.

[06:15] Miguel Santos (Redwood): For dot-product rerank we typically do a batched matrix multiply. On our Dedicated GPUs, batch size 64/128 for 512-dims gives best throughput while keeping p95 under 120-150 ms depending on kernel. For 256 dims you hit much better latency — p95 can drop to 70-100 ms for similar batch. There's variance by hardware (A10 vs A100).
[07:45] Maya Chen (Acme): We're worried about tail latency when burst QPS hits 100+. Do you recommend autoscaling or pre-warming?

[08:20] Miguel Santos (Redwood): Autoscaling helps but if you need strict p99 tail SLOs, Dedicated with reserved capacity plus burst lanes is safer. Also KV cache for prefix caching helps if you have session-like patterns — reduces re-compute. For reranking, caching embeddings or partial dot-products can help if queries repeat or candidates overlap.
[09:50] Tom Rivers (Acme): For VPC/on-prem, any constraints around kernel-level optimizations or quantization toolchain? We prefer to keep things air-gapped in our secure environment.

[10:30] Miguel Santos (Redwood): We support Private deployments; kernel selection and quantized runtime ship as part of the package. Quantized models (8-bit, 4-bit) require calibration but run fine on our runtime; we provide quantization profiles. On-prem install requires we validate GPU driver versions and CUDA/cuDNN compat but we can provide a validated matrix.
[12:05] Raj Patel (Acme): Can you share numbers for 128/256/512 dims for cost per 1M queries and latency ballpark?

[12:30] Lena Park (Redwood): We'll send the spreadsheet but high-level: 512 dims on hosted cheaper per-GB storage but higher compute cost — roughly 2.5-3x the cost of 128 dims on same throughput. On Dedicated, you amortize GPU better, so cost delta narrows. For per-query cost it depends on batching and reuse. We'll attach a delta table.

[13:45] Miguel Santos (Redwood): Example: on an A10 pool, 512-d dot-product rerank with batch 128 -> p50 30 ms, p95 140 ms; batch 64 -> p95 180 ms. 256-d batch 128 -> p95 around 90-110 ms. These are illustrative, we'll run with your exact models and seq lengths.
[15:00] Maya Chen (Acme): What about quantization quality? We can't afford big hit in rerank precision (NDCG).

[15:30] Miguel Santos (Redwood): Usually 8-bit quantization is almost lossless for embeddings and dot-product; post-training quant (4-bit) can be risky depending on distribution. For reranking we recommend evaluating 8-bit first with calibration. Our Optimize toolkit provides suggestions and a quality monitor so we can set regression alerts per prompt set.
[17:20] Raj Patel (Acme): How does KV cache help here? Our rerank stage is stateless per query but candidate lists overlap a lot between sessions.

[18:05] Miguel Santos (Redwood): If candidates overlap, caching embeddings or precomputed candidate vectors and partial similarity results reduces compute. Cache hit patterns matter; we can simulate hit rates with your logs. Cache TTL and invalidation tie to your indexing cadence.
[20:00] Tom Rivers (Acme): Security — SSO, KMS, audit logs — does Private give us full control of keys?
[20:30] Lena Park (Redwood): Private allows customer-managed KMS/HSM. Audit logs are plumbed to your logging endpoint; we support SAML/SSO and RBAC. We'll attach SOC2 and architecture docs.
[22:10] Maya Chen (Acme): For the POC, what do we need to run to get useful head-to-head numbers?

[22:35] Miguel Santos (Redwood): Give us sample queries, labeled ground truth, and a candidate set. We'll run experiments: dims 128/256/512, quantization 32/8-bit, batch sizes 32/64/128 on A10 and A100 configs. We'll report p50/p95/p99 and cost per million queries. Also compute NDCG and MRR regressions.
[24:00] Raj Patel (Acme): Timeline? We want results in two weeks if possible.

[24:15] Lena Park (Redwood): We can aim for a 10 business day turnaround once we have the dataset and access. We'll need a short workback plan and a pilot token for hosted or a small Dedicated slice for accurate numbers.
[26:00] Maya Chen (Acme): Any gotchas with embedding dimension reduction — e.g., retraining vs PCA?

[26:30] Miguel Santos (Redwood): If you compress via PCA or product quantization you must re-evaluate ranking. Distillation to lower-dim models or using a smaller embedding model is often better than aggressive post-hoc reduction. We'll test both approaches.
[28:40] Tom Rivers (Acme): For on-prem deployment can we restrict the runtime to certain PCIe lanes or driver versions?

[29:05] Miguel Santos (Redwood): We provide an install checklist. We do not normally lock to PCIe lanes but the hardware matrix will be validated; some kernel optimizations are sensitive to driver versions which we document.
[31:50] Maya Chen (Acme): We saw weird transcribe issues with vendor names in past calls, fwiw.
[32:00] Lena Park (Redwood): Noted, thanks. We'll share the benchmark sheet link here: https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/ACME-emb-rerank-2026.csv (access controlled).
[33:40] Raj Patel (Acme): Good. On costing: what levers do we have short term?

[34:10] Miguel Santos (Redwood): Short term: reduce dims, batching tuning, caching. Mid-term: move rerank to Dedicated pools or use quantized model variants. Also consider a hybrid approach: use cheap dot-product filter then an expensive cross-encoder only for top 10.
[36:00] Maya Chen (Acme): That hybrid sounds promising — reduce calls to the expensive model.

[37:20] Miguel Santos (Redwood): Right — many customers use two-stage: vector DB -> cheap dot-product rerank -> cross-encoder on top-k. Redwood routing supports that with per-route SLOs and automatic fallback.
[39:40] Tom Rivers (Acme): Any reference deployments in healthcare you can share?
[40:00] Lena Park (Redwood): We have anonymized case studies and a security pack; we'll share the relevant ones and make an intro to our compliance team if needed.
[42:10] Raj Patel (Acme): Ok let's recap next steps.

[42:25] Lena Park (Redwood): Recap: Redwood to run benchmarks across dims/quant/batch, share cost model, and provide Dedicated pilot options. Acme to provide sample queries/dataset and SLOs. Schedule pilot planning next week.
[43:05] Maya Chen (Acme): Sounds good. Any blockers from Redwood side?
[43:20] Miguel Santos (Redwood): No blockers — just need the data and a contact for secure transfer. We'll provision a test pool and start runs once we have access.
[44:00] Raj Patel (Acme): Thanks everyone, we'll circulate the dataset and schedule the follow-up.
[44:12] Lena Park (Redwood): Thanks all, we'll send the sheet and security docs. Bye.
[44:20] (call ended)
